abstract.p: With the high rate of deforestation and forest degradation in both rural and urban Uganda, understanding societal (youth) opinions regarding the state of affairs is vital. This study examined preferred ecosystems services and perceived satisfaction with the urban forestry and green spaces on urban livelihood, welfare, resilience, and environmental sustainability in four Ugandan cities: Kampala, Fort Portal, Mbarara, and Gulu. It explored the factors associated with youth satisfaction regarding the number of urban green spaces and parks. This study surveyed 501 responses using an online questionnaire, which were subjected to descriptive and ordered logit regression analysis. Descriptive results revealed that, whereas about 66% of participants expressed satisfaction with current urban parks, about 70% were keenly engaged in urban initiatives. A noteworthy 99% of the respondents expressed support for increased investment in green spaces and parks. The regression results demonstrated that Ugandan youths’ satisfaction with city green spaces and parks is predominantly driven by quality over quantity. A preference for biodiversity services was positively and very significantly connected to public satisfaction with the number of greenery spaces. On the contrary, a preference for air quality benefits echoed un-met ecological prospects, leading to lower satisfaction. Youths’ quality expectations appeared as the single most powerful predictor of satisfaction. Likewise, vigorous public participation in tree planting, vibrant youth outdoor engagement, and women’s involvement positively and significantly enhanced public satisfaction with the number of greenery spaces. Ultimately, urban investments and environmental awareness campaigns did not directly relate to satisfaction. Apart from income, demographics did not show any significant association with satisfaction. Urban planners in Uganda ought to focus on society-centered, biodiversity-rich, and functionally maintained urban forestry strategies.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Worldwide, urban forestry and green space ecosystem services face multiple obstacles, and Uganda demonstrates how these barriers prevent the effective management and development of urban green spaces [1,2,3,4,5,6,7]. These issues include management and planning for urban nature concerning the city/urban population [6,8,9,10]. Urban development, because of population expansion and industrial activities, has created major land transformations, which have reduced the number and quality of urban green spaces and the provided ecosystem services [4,5,6,8,11,12,13,14,15]. Moreover, climate change and tree diseases also play a significant role in the success of urban nature, particularly in relation to trees [16].

The health and accessibility of urban forests and green areas in Kampala are severely challenged by issues such as deforestation, inadequate waste management, and poor urban planning. The absence of sufficient funding for green spaces, combined with economic conditions and management issues, creates a situation where vulnerable populations suffer additional disadvantages in urban areas [7,17,18,19]. Addressing urban forest ecosystem service challenges requires a multifunctional approach with intensive planning and decision-making mechanisms and frameworks [11,17,20,21,22,23,24,25].

Globally, urban livelihood, especially the health of the citizens, essentially depends on urban parks and greenery for recreational activities, including exercising for physical and mental health [25,26,27,28,29,30,31]. Furthermore, urban society depends on the outside environment for general social and communal activities, hence serving as a uniting factor. Urban forestry became more important than ever during the COVID-19 pandemic as it became necessary for urban dwellers to go to nature for physical exercise and sunbathing for health benefits [19,32,33,34,35,36,37,38,39,40].

Research on the various functions of urban green spaces demonstrates their impact on community wellness, environmental resilience, and sustainability [26,31,37]. Numerous research studies have shown that access to green spaces is associated with improved physical and mental health outcomes [19,31,41,42,43,44,45,46,47,48]. Urban green areas serve as locations for exercise, socializing, and recreational activities, which help build community unity and create better urban environments. COVID-19 presented a case study of the social and health benefits of urban green spaces from around the globe [19,41,42,43,44,45,46,47,48]. Urban forests are vital to ecological health because they remove air pollution while cooling cities through temperature reduction and supporting biodiversity [8,49].

Urban dwellers’ support for the essential role of urban green spaces, parks, and forests is based on their fundamental importance to urban existence, encompassing both ecological functions and socioeconomic roles, such as energy and food security [27,31,49].

Research reveals that urban communities are increasingly aware of the environmental and health benefits generated by urban greening programs [19,27,50]. Furthermore, the participation of residents in tree planting, urban greening, and recreation, combined with environmental health, can develop their sense of ownership toward natural resources, thereby boosting environmental and livelihood resilience [7,19,25,51]. Sustainable urban development requires this kind of communal commitment.

The successful improvement of urban forestry requires the implementation of stakeholder collaboration, sustainable practices, and increased investment in green space initiatives. Urban greenery integration during the planning stages enhances ecological resilience and promotes social well-being, ensuring cities remain vibrant and livable for all residents despite global challenges. Cities must establish environmental stewardship through urban green spaces, as this approach will lead to sustainable community development and improved urban quality of life [8,49,50].

While stakeholders in many Ugandan cities seem to understand the role of urban forestry and green spaces, little has been studied to shed more light on the situation. Moreover, the number and quality of green spaces in many Ugandan cities are questionable, given their degradation in the country, including urban regions [8,49,50].

Additionally, Ugandan cities still face many challenges from the governance of land, and subsequently, the urban forestry and other green spaces, which are victims of poor governance and lack of proper property rights, industrialization and expansion, and limited innovation necessary for environmental resilience and sustainability [7,19,51,52,53]. More so, issues of land, forestry and gender, such as women’s participation in decision-making regarding land or forest-related activities, are faced with limitations and challenges, including demand for wood fuel, such as charcoal and firewood, even in urban settings in Uganda [54,55,56,57].

Land in urban Uganda is fragmented across multifaceted tenure arrangements, such as Mailo, customary, freehold, and public leases. This limits municipal/city land attainment for public greenery and parks. The land economic value factor is meant to reflect the dynamics of property values and rising prices that determine and push for rapid private development projects over public green space conservation. Moreover, land questions in Uganda, both rural and urban, have eminent ownership problems that equally affect urban greeneries and parks. Cases of land grabbing of public land for economic development are more rampant than ever [8,49,50].

Therefore, this study is timely and vital to understand the opinions of Ugandans regarding the state of urban forests and green spaces in major Ugandan cities. Moreover, it offers a way forward to make relevant policy decisions to improve and sustain urban nature given the numerous purposes it serves to society and environmental sustainability [58,59,60,61].

This study examined preferred ecosystem services and perceived satisfaction with the urban forestry and green spaces considering their impact on urban livelihood, welfare, resilience, and environmental sustainability in four Ugandan cities: Kampala, Fort Portal, Mbarara, and Gulu. It explored the factors affecting public satisfaction with urban forestry and green spaces, surveying 501 responses. Furthermore, this study aimed to contribute to the ongoing discourse on urban studies and sustainable development, as well as the livelihood of urban society in Uganda and beyond. The results express potential pathways for policy direction and further research.

p.italic: Appreciating urban biodiversity increases public satisfaction with the number of urban green spaces/parks and urban forestry, whereas intensified demand for air quality abatement is negatively related with satisfaction because of unmet ecological prospects in urban hubs.
Active public participation in greening initiatives and inclusive infrastructure design for youth and women significantly increase overall public satisfaction with urban greenery.
A perceived quality of green spaces meeting user expectations has a positive and dominant association with public satisfaction with the number of urban parks and green spaces.

sec.title: 2. Materials and Methods
sec.p: This study employed both qualitative and quantitative approaches, given the reliability of mixed methods [62,63,64,65]. The qualitative part included consulting previous studies, mainly from Scopus and Web of Science, which formed the foundation of this study. Moreover, the study gap and data collection tool were also based on the existing literature. The quantitative part was based on the coded data from the study questionnaire results and analysis outcomes, which have been tabulated, analyzed, and presented herein.

A mixed-methods research approach, combining qualitative and quantitative methods, enabled this study to gain a deeper understanding of the diverse elements affecting urban green space satisfaction. The combined research approach yielded stronger and more comprehensive results, which enhanced the validity and practical value of this study [66,67,68].

The quantitative analysis used survey questions that allowed participants to express their opinions. This research method enables researchers to gain a comprehensive understanding of the explanations behind people’s satisfaction or dissatisfaction with green spaces [66,67,68]. The findings from the qualitative data helped this study identify essential variables for the quantitative model, thereby facilitating a better understanding of the key influences affecting opinions on urban green space [66,67,68].

The quantitative results benefited from the existing literature because it helped identify specific characteristics that are associated with satisfaction scores in regression analysis. The combination of qualitative outcomes with quantitative data yielded a deeper understanding of multifaceted relationships in this study [66,67,68,69,70].

Moreover, this research employed quantitative descriptive analysis and ordered logit model regression to investigate how various factors are associated with satisfaction levels with urban green spaces. Furthermore, the approach permitted this study to measure and quantify satisfaction with the number of urban greeneries and parks and the relationship with environmental benefits, preferences, and socioeconomic characteristics [69,70].

sec.title: 2.1. Data Collection
sec.p: A non-probability convenience sampling method was employed to obtain online responses from the districts of Kampala, Mbarara, Fort Portal, and Gulu in Uganda. A significant majority of responses were obtained from Mbarara City and Kampala Capital City.
Kampala is the capital city of Uganda (0.3476° N, 32.5825° E), while Mbarara (−0.6042° S, 30.6564° E), Gulu (2.7747° N, 32.2991° E), and Fort Portal (0.6686° N, 30.2709° E) follow in that order.

Data were collected from 501 respondents through an online questionnaire (software Survio) employed for one month (28 February 2025 to 30 March 2025), with about a 56% response completion rate. The questionnaire was launched at the end of February, and the data were obtained through March 2025. The questionnaire had undergone quality tests, including expert review and pretesting. The final version was shared on various social media platforms for data collection.

This study shared a survey link through social media among networks such as Facebook, X, and WhatsApp contacts for quick and cost-effective data collection. The questionnaire was carefully structured and was approved as required. Ethical obligations were observed; consent from respondents was sought before filling out the questionnaire. The questionnaire was set according to quality requirements and obligations, such as one person per response, to avoid numerous responses that could distort the data. The limitations associated with online data collection are discussed in the Discussion section.
Data from the pretesting exercise were deleted to ensure the uniformity and quality of the data collected.

Demographic attributes of the respondents, including gender, age, income, education, and employment status, were also collected to facilitate a comprehensive analysis of their perceptions (Figure 1), to identify any gaps in the perceived inclusion of youth and women in urban forestry initiatives.

Approximately 58% (291) of the respondents were male, and about 42% (210) were female. The majority of respondents, 256, were between 18 and 25 years of age (approximately 50%), and about 41% (203) were between 26 and 35 years of age (Figure 1).

The majority of respondents (382) held a bachelor’s degree (approximately 76.2%), followed by a master’s degree (about 11%) and secondary school education (about 8%). The majority of the respondents were both employed and students, accounting for about 47% (234) and 43% (213), respectively. About 11% were unemployed (Figure 1).

Approximately 35% (175) of responses were obtained from Kampala, 56% *(282) from Mbarara, 6% (28) from Fort Portal, and 3 (16) from Gulu. Given the unequal representativeness of responses by city, the analysis focused on all the cities in general for a comparative analysis.

This study evaluated youth perceptions regarding urban parks, green spaces, and forestry initiatives within their city:
Most important urban greenery and forest ecosystems (biodiversity, water regulation, air quality improvement, land value, climate regulation, noise reduction, and recreation).
Quality of urban forestry, satisfaction with parks and green spaces, participation in urban greenery.
Investment in green spaces and urban forestry for youth, utilization of urban green spaces, stimulus for youth outdoor activities, youth and women in urban forestry resourcefulness.
Urban trees and air quality perception.

Lastly, the collected data were cleaned, coded (Table 1), and subjected to descriptive and inferential statistical analysis to identify the main trends and ratios necessary for policy advice and future studies. The variables have been explained to understand the connection between the variables and the study questions as well as the measurement. Most correlations were positive and weak or moderate. The two-tailed analysis showed a critical value (0.0876) at 5%, and coefficients with absolute values above this threshold are statistically significant; those below it are not (Table 2).

The two-tailed analysis showed a critical value (0.0876) at 5%, and coefficients with absolute values above the threshold are statistically significant. The strongest observed association was between those satisfied with the number of parks and green spaces in the city (Satisfied-NPGS) and the quality of urban forestry in the city meeting expectations (QoUFG-Expect) [at approximately 0.8] (Table 2).

This connection does not impact the regression given that one is the dependent variable (Satisfied-NPGS) and the other independent. The other moderately positive relations included the preference for water regulation (WaterReg) with the preference for biodiversity protection (Biodiversity) [about 0.4], the preference for water regulation (WaterReg) with the quality of urban forestry in the city meeting expectations (QoUFG-Expect) [approximately 0.4], and the preference for biodiversity protection (Biodiversity) with those satisfied with the number of parks and green spaces in the city (Satisfied-NPGS) [around 0.4]. The rest of the variables scored marginal correlations (Table 2).

sec.title: 2.2. Data Analysis Method
sec.p: The cleaned and coded data were analyzed for descriptive statistics to illustrate patterns, trends, and disparities in the results. More so, descriptive statistics offer an easier understanding of study data, relate groups or observations, and present the main findings clearly with tables and graphs.

The analysis started with conducting correlation examination to detect any multicollinearity diagnosis. There were no severe correlational problems observed, and hence the variables were suitable for analysis, as most correlations were positive and weak or moderate (Table 2).

Given that SatisfiedNPGS is the dependent variable, the current correlation with QoUFGExpect (0.8) did not show multicollinearity among the other predictors. It specified a strong relationship between the result and that predictor, which is fundamentally significant for this study (Table 2).

sec.title: 2.3. Ordered Logit Model Regression Method
sec.p: We used an ordered logit model regression method, which was applied because of this study’s categorical and ranking measurements and the intervals between categories.

Based on the proportional odds assumption, it evaluates a single set of regression coefficients (β represents beta) across all group thresholds, sustaining the model simplicity and interpretation through proportional odds ratios. The ordered logit model is widely used across experiential disciplines where survey ratings, such as Likert scales, or ordered categorizations serve as the dependent variable [69,70].

Other methods, such as typical multinomial logit, disregard the ordinal construction of the data, whereas ordinary least squares regression adopts an equivalent arrangement amongst categories such as “Strongly Disagree, Disagree, Neutral, Agree and Strongly Agree” [69,70].

Model Specification Logit (P(Yi ≤ k ⃓ Xi)) = αk − β ˕ Xi, k = 1, …, K − 1 where αk denotes the k-th cut-point threshold (α1 < α2 … < αk − 1), and β is the vector of estimated parameters across p covariates Xi. Exponentiated coefficients (exp βj) represent proportional odds ratios (OR), where OR > 1 indicates higher odds of attaining a higher outcome category as predictor Xj increases.

Model 1 characterized the full ordered logit specification comprising all explanatory variables (N = 501). The model revealed strong generally statistical acceptability (likelihood ratio = 635.108, p < 0.001, and R2 = 42.1%), and correctly predicted 58.3% cases. Satisfied-NPGS is the dependent variable, representing satisfaction with the number of parks and green spaces in the city.

Model 2 decreased eight statistically inconsequential variables (i.e., Climatereg, Recreation, NoiseRed, InvestMIGSUF, GSPUseRecreati, Utrees AirQ, Education, and Employment) to advance model strength with improved efficiency.

Given the experiential results provided in Model 2, outcomes displayed a robust statistical fit and presentation across all key diagnostic standards (correctly predicted 58.5% of cases). Lower values for AIC (915.922 vs. 924.345, Model 1), BIC (991.821 vs. 1029.760, Model 1), and HQIC (945.702 vs. 965.706, Model 1) indicate a superior model performance with less risk of overfitting. Model 2 is superior to Model 1 across all three information criteria. The general requirement was highly significant with the likelihood ratio test (R = 629.531, and p < 0.001). More so, the model attained a McFadden Pseudo R2 of 41.7%, representing a substantial explanatory influence above the typical threshold for well-fitting ordinal models (Table 3).

Both Model 3 and 4 conditions confirmed a robust general statistical goodness of fit, demonstrating likelihood ratio tests confirming mutual significance at p < 0.001 (627.873 for Model 3 and 528.342 for Model 4 respectively). Model 3 produced a McFadden Pseudo R2 of 41.6% and an Adjusted R2 of 40.14%, demonstrating a remarkably high explanatory influence for ordinal conditions. In contrast, Model 4 noted a McFadden Pseudo R2 of 37.13% and an Adjusted R2 of 35.87%.

A relative assessment identified Model 3 as the optimal specification, as it revealed lower values across the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) = 911.58 vs. 920.561, Schwarz Criterion (BIC) = 974.829 vs. 975.377, and Hannan–Quinn Criterion (HQIC) = 936.396 vs. 942.069. Likewise, Model 3 established superior analytical accuracy, correctly classifying 58.5% of cases compared to 56.9% (Model 4). Therefore, Model 3 is reserved as the principal preference model for practical clarification and discussion.

sec.title: 3. Results
sec.p: Collectively, 65.8% of youths stated satisfaction with urban parks and green spaces, i.e., very satisfied plus satisfied. While 27% articulated dissatisfaction with the state of the green spaces, forestry, and trees in their cities (Table 4). This survey revealed a largely positive view of the accessibility, availability, and quality of green spaces and parks in Uganda; however, a noteworthy proportion remains dissatisfied, highlighting an area for improvement.

The majority of the results, i.e., 66.5% of the youths, showed that urban forestry and green spaces met their expectations. This suggests that city youths appreciate the status of the existing trees and green spaces. Conversely, 22.8% of youths disagreed or felt neutral, indicating that aspects of urban forestry and green spaces needed improvements (Table 4).

The study outcomes showed that 69.7% of participants often engaged in urban gardening or tree-planting activities. This demonstrated strong public engagement in increasing and improving local greenery and forests. Only 13.6% of the respondents participated rarely or never in joint initiatives, confirming a strong interest in environmental and ecological initiatives (Table 5).

An overwhelming majority of 98.8% supported and suggested increased investment in green spaces and urban forestry, with a focus on youth (Table 5). This suggested a robust consensus among other society members on the significance of urban green spaces for youth, highlighting a potential priority for urban planners and policymakers.

The outcomes revealed that a substantial 80.4% of respondents frequently utilized green spaces and parks for recreational activities (Table 5). This suggests that urban green spaces, forestry, and street trees are vital for community lifestyle, welfare, and social connections. A low fraction of non-users was observed, suggesting a primarily active commitment to outdoor recreational services.

A remarkable 98.5% of respondents believed that urban trees and/or forestry have a positive impact on air quality (Table 6). Thus, this indicates a strong public understanding of the benefits and services provided by urban forestry and trees to environmental and ecological ecosystems.

The results illustrated that 91.7% of respondents agreed that urban greenery boosts youth outdoor involvement (Table 7). This suggests that urban planning and policymaking should prioritize the attractiveness of urban green spaces and parks to promote and enhance the active lifestyles of the city’s youth. Urban greenery and forests in the city encourage youth to spend more time outdoors.

The outcomes of the survey about youth and women’s perspectives on urban forestry and green space programs and activities are worth examining. The results showed that the majority of respondents, at 81.3%, agreed that urban forestry and green space initiatives included youth and gender perspectives, while 9.4% remained neutral or disagreed, suggesting disengagement (Table 7).

sec.title: 3.1.1. Models 1 and 2
sec.p: The ordered logit model that assessed the factors associated with the satisfaction with the number of parks, urban forestry, and green spaces (NPGS) revealed a good fit as per the likelihood ratio test (Chi-square = 635.108, p < 0.001, [Model 1, Table 3]). This means that the model is a better predictor of satisfaction levels than a null model with no predictors (Model 1).

Preference for climate regulation: A non-significant and positive association was found between the importance of climate regulation as an urban forest service and the level of satisfaction with the number of parks and green spaces (coefficient = 0.110, p < 0.598).
Prefer biodiversity protection: A positive relationship was found between satisfaction and the preference for biodiversity protection (coefficient = 0.486, p < 0.028).
Preference for land value increase: There showed a negative and non-significant connection between preference for land value increase and satisfaction (coefficient = −0.200, p < 0.344).

The preference for water regulation and preference for recreation services were negatively and non-significantly related to satisfaction (coefficient = −0.200, p < 0.359, and coefficient = −0.242, p < 0.213, respectively). The result for preference for recreation services was similar to the preference for water regulation, negative and non-significant.
On the other hand, the preference for air quality improvement was negative and non-significantly associated with satisfaction with urban forestry and green spaces in Ugandan cities (model 1).

Urban greenery expectations: Individuals with higher expectations of urban greenery were very significantly and positively associated with satisfaction with green spaces and urban forestry (coefficient = 1.703, p < 0.001).

The impact of urban forestry and green spaces on quality of life: A highly significant and negative correlation was found between the belief that urban forestry and green spaces impact on the quality of life of all residents and satisfaction (coefficient = −0.528, p < 0.017 [Table 8]).

Respondents’ participation in urban greening activities and urban greeneries’ youth outdoor orientation were both positive and significantly highly associated with satisfaction with the number of green spaces, parks or forests in the city (coefficient = −0.528, p < 0.017). More so, perceived inclusion of youth and women in urban greenery or parks had a positive and moderate association with the satisfaction with the number of parks in Uganda (Table 8).

The need to invest more in urban greeneries, greenery use/recreation use, and awareness about urban greenery and forestry were found to be positively and non-significantly correlated, indicating that respondents were likely to be satisfied (Model 1).

Urban trees and greenery’s role in improving air quality belief in Ugandan cities was negative and non-significantly associated with satisfaction with the number of green spaces, parks or forests in the city (Table 8).

Regarding demographics, income age and employment were positive but not significantly related with satisfaction with the number of green spaces, parks or forests in the city. Meanwhile, gender and education were negative but not significantly related with satisfaction with the number of green spaces, parks or forests in the city (Model 1).

sec.title: 3.1.2. Model 2
sec.p: Similarly, prioritizing biodiversity protection was positive, and strongly significantly associated with satisfaction with the number of green spaces, parks or forests in the city (coefficient = 0.521, p < 0.016). This further supports the importance of ecological value in determining perceptions of green space adequacy (Model 2, Table 8).

Air quality preference showed a negative but moderately significant correlation between air quality services of urban forest/green spaces and satisfaction (coefficient = −0.431, p < 0.099) (Model 2, Table 8).
Preferences for water regulation services and land value increase were negative and non-significant (Model 2, Table 8).

Urban greenery and green space expectations regarding the quality of life were positively and strongly significantly related to satisfaction with the number of sites of urban greenery and parks (coefficient = (1.670, p < 0.001)).

Urban forestry and greenery’s perceived impact on the quality of life demonstrated a negative and strong significant correlation with satisfaction with the number of green spaces/parks or forestry (coefficient = −0.509, p < 0.016).

Perceived awareness about the importance of urban greenery and forestry showed a positive but non-significant association with satisfaction with the number of sites of urban greenery and forestry (coefficient = 0.289, p < 0.243).

Respondents’ participation in urban greening activities and an urban greenery youth outdoor orientation were both positive and significantly highly associated with satisfaction with the number of green spaces, parks or forests in the city (Model 2, Table 8). More so, perceived inclusion of youth and women in urban greenery or parks had a positive and moderate association with the satisfaction with the number of parks in Uganda (Model 2, Table 8).

Demographic characteristics were generally positive but non-significant (gender and income), while age had a negative and non-significant relationship with the satisfaction with the number of parks in Uganda (Model 2, Table 8).

sec.title: 3.1.3. Model 3
sec.p: Air quality improvement preference, as an urban forest service, had a negative but significant association with the satisfaction with the number of parks in Uganda (coefficient = −0.455, p < 0.08). This suggests that people who value the environmental benefits of green spaces are less likely to be satisfied with their availability (Model 3, Table 9).
Land value increase as an urban forest service had a negative and non-significant relationship with satisfaction (coefficient = −0.192, p = 0.351).

Biodiversity protection was positive, and it was strongly significantly associated with satisfaction with urban forestry and green spaces (coefficient = 0.515, p < 0.013). This further emphasizes the importance of ecological value in shaping perceptions of green space adequacy.
Higher expectations regarding urban greenery were strongly positive and highly significantly linked to increased satisfaction with urban forestry (coefficient = 1.669, p < 0.001).

There was a negative relationship between the impact of urban forestry and green spaces on quality of life and satisfaction with the number of sites of urban forestry and green spaces (coefficient = −0.476, p < 0.022). This suggests that people who value the environmental benefits of green spaces are less likely to be satisfied with their current state.

Respondents’ participation in urban greening activities and an urban greenery youth outdoor orientation (coefficient = 0.388, p < 0.001 and coefficient = 0.489, p < 0.003, respectively) were both positive and significantly highly associated with satisfaction with the number of green spaces, parks or forests in the city (Model 3, Table 9). More so, perceived inclusion of youth and women in urban greenery (coefficient = 0.242, p < 0.081) or parks had a positive and moderate association with the satisfaction with the number of parks in Uganda (Model 3, Table 9).

Increased awareness needed about urban greenery and forestry was positively but not significantly associated with the number of sites of urban forestry and green spaces (coefficient = 0.298, p = 0.23).
Gender was negatively and non-significantly associated with satisfaction with green spaces and urban forestry (coefficient = −0.148, p = 0.434 [Model 3, Table 9]).

The relationship between income and satisfaction with the number of sites of urban forestry and green spaces was positive and very significant (coefficient = 0.182, p < 0.041). This suggested that individuals with higher incomes may have different perceptions or access to green spaces that contribute to their satisfaction. The result equally demonstrates the possibility of dissatisfaction for lower-income earners with urban greeneries given other factors, such as access restrictions.

sec.title: 3.1.4. Model 4
sec.p: A higher perceived quality of life enhanced by the urban forestry and greenery was negatively and very significantly (Coefficient: −0.289 and p-value = 0.017) associated with a decrease in satisfaction with the number of parks, forests, and green spaces (Model 4, Table 9). The negative coefficient indicates that people who rate the quality of life in urban areas highly may feel that the available green spaces are insufficient.

Higher expectations regarding urban greenery were strongly positive and very significantly connected with an increase in satisfaction with the number of parks, forests, and green spaces (Coefficient: 0.92 and p-value = 0.001). This showed that people who have high expectations of urban greenery tend to be satisfied with the current level of greenery (Model 4, Table 9).

The level of participation in urban greenery initiatives had a strongly positive and very significant association with the level of satisfaction with the number of parks, forests, and green spaces (Coefficient: 0.182 and p-value: 0.009). This means that such activities can improve the level of satisfaction (Model 4, Table 7).

The focus on urban greenery for youth outdoor activities had a strong, positive, and very significant relationship with satisfaction with the number of parks, forests, and green spaces (Coefficient: 0.252, p-value: 0.005).

Urban Greenery Includes Youth and Women: The perception that that the city’s urban forestry and greenery initiatives include the input and perspectives of youth and women had a positive and significant association with the satisfaction with the number of parks, forests, and green spaces (Coefficient: 0.196, p-value = 0.011).

Variables ‘invest more in urban greenery’, ‘greenery use for recreation’, and ‘awareness needed about urban greenery and forestry’ were found have positive but non-significant associations with satisfaction with the number of parks, forests, and green spaces (Model 4, Table 9).

There was a non-significant relationship between believing that urban trees improve air quality and dissatisfaction with the number of parks, forests, and green spaces (Coefficient: −0.024 and p-value: 0.837). This might imply that people who appreciate the role of trees in improving air quality still complain that there are not enough green spaces to address the air quality problem.

This study found Model 3 to be the optimal specification, because it showed lower values across the Akaike Information Criterion (911.58 vs. 920.561), Schwarz Criterion (974.829 vs. 975.377), and Hannan–Quinn Criterion (936.396 vs. 942.069). Furthermore, Model 3 demonstrated a greater analytical accuracy (58.5% of cases) compared to Model 4 (56.9%). Consequently, this study chose Model 3 as the primary preference model for concrete explanation and argument.

sec.title: 4. Discussion
sec.p: The study results emphasized the critical role and benefits of green spaces, urban parks, and forestry initiatives and mechanisms in improving community well-being and promoting environmental stewardship [71,72,73]. Most of the respondents expressed positive opinions about the quality and accessibility of Uganda’s urban green spaces, parks, and forests. This underlined the role and importance of urban nature as a vital fundamental of urban life [27,50]. The study opinions showed satisfactory facts necessary for efficient management of existing initiatives. Moreover, this study identified areas for improvement, primarily for city residents and neighborhoods that feel underserved, given the substantial benefits [74,75].

The significant public commitment and participation in urban nature and tree-planting activities exhibited an aspiration for involvement in urban environmental and ecological determinations and development [76,77,78]. This communal response stimulates a sense of public ownership and obligation, which is essential for the sustainability and resilience of urban environments. Moreover, the prominence of improved ventures in urban environments and ecological wellbeing, mainly for youth, has exhibited an extensive acknowledgement of the long-standing benefits that urban greeneries, forests, and parks deliver in promoting healthy lifestyles and resilient communities [36,79,80].

The youths’ strong opinions on the optimistic impact of urban trees/forests on air quality demonstrated a profound mindfulness of environmental matters, emphasizing the requirement of assimilating nature into urban planning and settings. The robust connection between accessibility of green environments and vigorous outdoor daily life among the Ugandan youth echoes the potential for urban environments and spaces to become promoters of social connections, physical and mental health, and educational prospects. As public health concerns continue to rise in cities globally, the inevitability of sustaining urban greenery, forests, and parks becomes increasingly apparent.

This study also identified positive and significant perceived inclusiveness of vulnerable groups, including youth and women, in urban forestry and greenery initiatives and mechanisms. While many youths believe their viewpoints are considered, a notable percentage expressed neutrality or disagreement. To address such concerns and issues, it is crucial to develop approaches and policies that are both inclusive and effective in meeting the various needs of urban society and neighborhoods [81,82]. Involving all stakeholder groups in planning and decision-making processes helps to achieve maximum and optimal results that are both desired and impactful. This will foster a strong connection between urban residents and their environment, promoting resilience and sustainability [82,83,84,85].

Likewise, this study showed a similar positive preference for ecological benefits as well as social benefits. The study findings noted that biodiversity preference was positive and very significantly associated with the number of green spaces in Ugandan cities. This study emphasized the significance of urban parks, forests, and other green spaces as essential community welfare (quality of life) mechanisms and environmental and ecological health [5,27].

This study noted a positive and non-significant association between the perceived need for investments in green spaces and urban forestry, awareness, and green space use/recreation, and the satisfaction with urban green spaces (Models 1, 2, and 3). The findings (98.5%) show that there is a need for investment in green space infrastructure, and they call for continuous, resilient, and increased investment in urban nature conservation, taking into account its multidimensional benefits. Furthermore, there is a need for comprehensive stakeholder participation that comprises all public members in the cities. By giving priority to the voices of youth, women, and other vulnerable groups in future urban forestry and greenery initiatives, cities and urban areas can nurture more lively, vibrant, sustainable, and resilient environments that promote a logic of fitting in or belonging, hence improving the quality of urban life and ensuring ecological and environmental sustainability.

The regression models (Models 1, 2, and 3) demonstrated that urban park satisfaction, greenery, and forestry depend on multiple environmental values, together with public expectations and anticipations. People who prefer biodiversity protection services as essential benefits of urban forests tend to be satisfied. The delivery and communication of ecological functions must be prioritized because they directly influence public and societal benefits and satisfaction [86,87,88,89,90]. The connection between urban green spaces and public expectations is a vital factor, as people tend to feel more satisfied when their expectations match or exceed reality [91].

The analysis revealed that socioeconomic variables have a direct impact on satisfaction levels, as higher income is associated with greater satisfaction, although this may be due to variations in access and quality [86,88,89]. More so, it could reflect the dissatisfaction from lower-income earners given other factors like accessibility due to pay or other restrictions such as membership.

The current study demonstrated that gender and education status demonstrated negative associations with satisfaction, which requires additional investigation to understand their underlying/basic grounds. This study indicated that urban green space planning must employ a comprehensive methodology by integrating environmental benefits with the diverse requirements and values of the urban community [76].

The second model (Model 2) demonstrated that environmental values and benefits, expectations, and socioeconomic perceptions (quality of life, expectations regarding the quality of green spaces) significantly influence satisfaction with urban green spaces and forestry. Higher satisfaction rates among residents emerge when biodiversity protection is prioritized, as these ecological advantages are considered most important [49,86,88,89,92,93,94].

Based on the optimal model (Model 3), this study noted a dynamic set of associations with satisfaction levels with the number of urban green spaces. Nonetheless, prioritizing biodiversity protection services and air quality benefits were more likely to increase satisfaction. While emphasizing the significance of ecological benefits, land value increase is likely to reduce satisfaction with the number of urban green spaces in Uganda. These informative findings deserve further investigation and study to determine why valuing these services may lead to dissatisfaction. Satisfaction is consistently higher for people who have higher expectations of urban greenery, suggesting that it is important to meet or exceed these expectations.

Ugandan city residents’ expectation vs. reality disconnect: The inverse coefficients of air quality and water regulation preferences can be explained through intellectual discord. City residents with high standard awareness of ecosystem services hold higher environmental standards. Given that Ugandan cities face seasonal air pollution and flooding, such high expectations clash with daily reality. This results in inferior or subjective satisfaction in comparison with less environmentally aware inhabitants [8,49,51,58,94,95,96].
The study findings agree with previous studies [97,98] on ecological and socioeconomics in Asia (China and Hong Kong).

Preference for ecological values shows that youths who appreciate urban green infrastructure as an important reserve for urban/city flora and fauna echo considerably higher general satisfaction with the quantity and accessibility of green spaces and parks or urban forests. In the setting of rapidly urbanizing states like Uganda as well as others in sub-Saharan Africa, where residents’ disintegration is common, youths place a high value on intact or biologically diverse ecosystems over homogenized or artificial green spots [51,99,100,101,102].

Perceived participation in urban greenery activities or even socializing in urban parks, among others, was seen to motivate public satisfaction. Other studies noted that just socializing outside in a park was motivating and encouraged satisfaction with the number and quality of green spaces [51,58,99,103].

Socioeconomic factors are also important in this context, with higher income being associated with higher satisfaction, which may reflect disparities in access or quality. Gender and education status, however, are negatively associated with satisfaction, suggesting that there may be differences in needs and/or opinions among these clusters [58,86,94,95,96].

Women/Gender Land Rights: While formal land rights in Uganda remain predominantly male-controlled, women and youth are the primary users of local environments. Isolating youth and women’s inclusion captures how participating in governance scholarships to non-landowning groups gives them a voice in spatial planning. Additionally, given the resource dependency in low-income city zones, green spaces provide direct livelihoods (such as fuel wood and urban agriculture). Therefore, municipal greening restrictions limit community access, hence negatively influencing local satisfaction [8,49,50,51,104,105].

Therefore, the model proposes that more sophisticated approaches are necessary to address the diverse values and expectations of people, thereby improving satisfaction with the number of urban green spaces.

sec.title: 4.1. Important Takeaway for Urban Planning
sec.p: The current results determined that ecological functionality rather than mere aesthetic greening motivates public satisfaction with urban green spaces. There, urban planning approaches in Ugandan cities ought to prioritize biodiversity-rich, native vegetation systems that provide quantifiable ecosystem services such as pollution filtration for air quality and microclimate regulation, water and soil.

Public satisfaction is essentially driven by quality over pure quantity and quality. Therefore, meeting youths’ expectations regarding maintenance, sanitation, safety, and changing green infrastructure into valued community resources is a necessary priority.

Urban greeneries in cities serve as vigorous sites for socialization. Involved planning that prioritizes safety, recreational user interface design for youth, and accessible space for women produces significant advantages in community satisfaction.
Civic engagement fosters psychological ownership and community stewardship. Encouraging hands-on participation converts passive park consumers into active guardians of urban greenery.

Investment is a necessary precondition for urban sustainability. Investment expenditure increases public satisfaction only when it directly translates into higher physical quality, increasing the number of green spaces and urban forests as well as maintaining them. Moreover, diversifying recreation facilities in parks requires financial and technical investments for both quality livelihoods and biodiversity ecosystem service sustainability.

Broad educational outreach generates the foundation for ecological appreciation and active community involvement. To maximize impact, educational and awareness programs ought to be paired with actionable possibilities for community tree planting and youth engagement.

sec.title: 4.2. Study Limitations
sec.p: Limited internet usage: This research recognizes and acknowledges mobile internet accessibility and coverage gaps. Moreover, digital access limitations relating to device accessibility and obtainability, energy, costs, and digital skills may exclude key stakeholders among the population.

Youth focus: This study cannot be generalized to the national population given its emphasis on the youth. This study stressed youth perspectives given Uganda’s young population, but it did not restrict admissibility to under 35 years (92% approximately); and hence the sample includes ages above 36 (about 8%), though a very small proportion.

Furthermore, the non-probability convenience sampling method limits the generalization of the study outcomes throughout all populations in Uganda. Even though this study suffered some limitations as mentioned, it followed survey techniques and recommendations as reported. Prospective research ought to employ stratified household assessments or mixed sampling methods focusing on all cities, or major ones, and general populations to validate and extend the current research outcomes.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: Despite the fundamental character and role of urban parks, forestry, and green spaces in providing and improving the quality of life in urban settings, there is a noteworthy gap in appreciating their significance. Moreover, comprehending public opinions and engagement in such initiatives and programs in Uganda is of paramount importance.

This study aimed to explore such perceptions of satisfaction with the number of sites of urban forestry and green spaces in Uganda. Moreover, this study assessed the level of community involvement, especially among youth and women, throughout the four cities of Kampala, Fort Portal, Mbarara, and Gulu in Uganda. We used an online survey questionnaire to gather (n = 501) responses. Data were cleaned, coded and analyzed for descriptive and ordered logit model results. The descriptive statistical findings revealed that, whereas about 66% of the participants expressed satisfaction with current urban parks, about 70% were keenly engaged in urban initiatives such as gardening and tree-planting activities. Additionally, a noteworthy 99% expressed support for improved investment in green spaces, demonstrating society’s awareness of the need for improvement and progress.

Model results demonstrated that urban park and green space satisfaction levels were strongly and positively associated with environmental values and services, expectations regarding the quality of urban green spaces, and socioeconomic factors such as involving the youth and women. Satisfaction increases when people prioritize ecological benefits, including biodiversity protection services. On the other hand, air quality benefits reflect unmet or current environmental expectations, leading to lower satisfaction levels.

Socioeconomic elements, including gender, employment, and education, were not significantly associated with satisfaction with the number of green spaces. However, income being positively associated with higher satisfaction may reflect disparities in access or quality, which may not cater for low-income earners’ dissatisfaction.

These model results demonstrated that city managers and development partners in Uganda should adopt an extensive and sensitive framework for urban green space development by considering environmental advantages together with diverse community needs and economic conditions.

This research demonstrated that public satisfaction with urban green spaces has multiple associated determinants. This study revealed that urban planners require sophisticated methods (multidimensional approach) for city development and policy creation.

Recommendations
Holistic Planning: Urban green space planning should use a comprehensive method that balances environmental advantages with the different needs and socioeconomic characteristics of community members.
Prioritize Ecological Benefits: The communication and management strategies for urban green spaces should focus on their ecological benefits, which include climate regulation and biodiversity protection.
Manage Expectations: Green space initiatives need clear goals and limited communications with stakeholders. Awareness campaigns should be combined with real improvements to prevent creating unattainable expectations.
Promote Community Engagement: Community involvement throughout the stages of green space planning, design, and maintenance boosts both ownership and satisfaction levels.
Addressing Disparities: Strategies are needed to reduce socioeconomic inequalities in green space accessibility and quality.
Tailored Approaches: Create specific solutions for distinct population segments based on gender and employment status, together with other demographic characteristics.
Continuous Improvement: The quality and accessibility of green spaces need periodic evaluation and enhancement to fulfill changing needs and public expectations.
